disclaimer: Ekseem Maar Net is a family passion project, made out of love for our brother. It is not a medical app. Everything here is general, surface-level information gathered from public guidelines and research, not medical advice. Eczema differs from person to person, so always speak to a doctor, dermatologist or pharmacist before starting, stopping or changing any treatment.

categories.title: Main Contributing Factors
categories.subtitle: The things that matter most, in order
categories.intro: Eczema comes from a leaky skin barrier and an over-reactive immune system, and it often runs in families. Food is rarely the root cause. The biggest wins come from daily skin care, treating flares early and avoiding everyday irritants.

items.name: Weak skin barrier
items.note: Eczema skin loses water and lets irritants and germs in. Daily moisturiser is the single most important habit.

items.name: Under-treated flares
items.note: Fear of steroid creams often means flares are treated too little, too late. Treating early with the right cream calms the skin faster.

items.name: Genes and family history
items.note: About 70% of people with eczema have a relative with eczema, asthma or hay fever. It is nobody's fault.

items.name: Over-reactive immune system
items.note: Allergy-type messengers (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31) cause redness and itch. The newest medicines block exactly these.

items.name: Staph bacteria
items.note: This common skin germ thrives on eczema patches and worsens flares. Treating the eczema reduces it.

items.name: The itch–scratch cycle
items.note: Scratching damages skin, which makes it itch more. Breaking the cycle is key: see habit reversal under Treatment.

items.name: Soaps, bubble bath and detergents
items.note: Anything that foams strips the skin barrier. Use a soap-free wash.

items.name: Fragrance and perfume
items.note: A common irritant and allergen in creams, washes and washing powder.

items.name: Stress
items.note: Stress makes itch worse, and eczema causes stress. Coping skills and support help (see Motivation).

items.name: Heat and sweat
items.note: Keep cool, rinse sweat off and moisturise. Don't stop sport or play.

items.name: Tobacco smoke
items.note: Second-hand smoke worsens eczema. Keep homes and cars smoke-free.

sections.title: Food: the facts
sections.intro: Every major guideline advises against cutting out foods "just in case". In one clinic, 19% of children on elimination diets developed new, sometimes severe allergies. Only remove a food if a doctor confirms an allergy.

items.name: Oats, wheat and gluten
items.note: No benefit from avoiding them unless coeliac disease or a wheat allergy is diagnosed.

items.name: Milk, cheese and butter
items.note: Fine unless a cow's milk allergy is diagnosed. Don't cut dairy without a dietitian, because children need calcium.

items.name: Yoghurt, amasi and maas
items.note: Fermented milk was linked to less eczema in South African toddlers.

items.name: Eggs
items.note: Eggs are not dairy. Egg is a common allergy in South African children with eczema, but only avoid it if an allergy is proven.

items.name: Nuts and peanuts
items.note: Not a cause in people who aren't allergic. Giving smooth peanut early (from 4–6 months) prevents peanut allergy. Whole nuts are a choking risk under 5.

items.name: Refined sugar
items.note: Sugar contains no histamine, and a challenge study showed it doesn't cause flares. Limit it for teeth and general health.

categories.title: Wonder Cures
categories.subtitle: Advanced treatments that are changing lives
categories.intro: None of these cures eczema, but for moderate–severe eczema they can bring long-lasting clear skin. They are prescription medicines chosen by a dermatologist, and still used alongside daily moisturiser. This page is just to know what exists, so ask your dermatologist whether any of them suits you.

items.name: Dupixent (dupilumab), injection
items.note: A biologic that blocks the IL-4/IL-13 allergy pathway, injected every 2–4 weeks. Registered in South Africa from 6 years (from 6 months in the US and EU). Main side effect: eye irritation. No routine blood tests.

items.name: Rinvoq (upadacitinib), daily tablet
items.note: A JAK inhibitor that works fast, with strong results in trials. Registered in South Africa from 12 years. It carries a boxed warning (infections, clots, heart events, cancer) and needs blood tests. No grapefruit.

items.name: Cibinqo (abrocitinib), daily tablet
items.note: A JAK inhibitor, registered in South Africa in April 2025 (from 12 years in the EU). It has the same JAK safety warnings and monitoring as Rinvoq.

sections.title: Approved overseas: ask your dermatologist
sections.intro: Approved in the US or EU, but South African registration was not confirmed when we checked.

items.name: Ebglyss (lebrikizumab), injection
items.note: An IL-13 biologic with monthly maintenance doses. From 12 years. Mostly causes conjunctivitis.

items.name: Adtralza / Adbry (tralokinumab), injection
items.note: An IL-13 biologic. From 12 years in the US.

items.name: Nemluvio (nemolizumab), injection
items.note: Targets the itch signal (IL-31) and gives fast itch relief. From 12 years.

items.name: Olumiant (baricitinib), tablet
items.note: A JAK inhibitor approved for eczema in the EU from 2 years. Same JAK warnings.

items.name: Opzelura (ruxolitinib cream)
items.note: The first JAK cream, approved in the US from 2 years (Sept 2025). Use it short-term on limited areas.

items.name: Zoryve (roflumilast cream)
items.note: A once-daily non-steroid cream. US approval from 2 years (Oct 2025).

items.name: Vtama (tapinarof cream)
items.note: A once-daily non-steroid cream. US approval from 2 years. May cause folliculitis (about 9%).

items.name: Anzupgo (delgocitinib cream)
items.note: For adults with chronic hand eczema (US, July 2025).

items.name: Amlitelimab
items.note: A new kind of injection (OX40 ligand) that may need dosing only every 12 weeks. Phase 3 results are mixed, with filings expected in late 2026.

items.name: Rocatinlimab
items.note: Trials were stopped in March 2026 after safety concerns.

categories.title: Treatment
categories.subtitle: What doctors recommend, step by step
categories.intro: Every major guideline (AAD, NICE, European and South African) uses the same steps. Moisturise every day. Treat flares early with the right-strength anti-inflammatory cream. Then prevent flares with twice-weekly use. Used correctly, steroid creams are safe and effective.

sections.title: The steps
sections.intro:
1. Every day, even when skin is clear: fragrance-free moisturiser on the whole body.
2. At the first sign of a flare: a steroid cream of the right strength (mild on the face) on the red patches.
3. Face, eyelids and folds: a steroid-free cream such as tacrolimus may suit better.
4. Once calm: use the cream twice a week on the usual spots to stop flares coming back.
5. Still not controlled? Ask about light therapy, tablets or injections (see Wonder Cures).

items.name: Moisturisers (emollients)
items.note: The foundation of all care. Use them daily on the whole body. Children need about 250–500 g a week. The best one is the one you'll actually use.

items.name: Fragrance-free products
items.note: Fragrance is one of the most common skin allergens. Choose unperfumed, dye-free products.

items.name: Petroleum jelly (Vaseline)
items.note: Cheap, effective and fragrance-free. Recommended in South African guidance when cost is an issue.

items.name: Aqueous cream as a moisturiser
items.note: It damages the skin barrier when left on. Only use it as a soap substitute, then rinse off.

items.name: Topical corticosteroids (steroid creams)
items.note: First choice for flares of any severity, at the right strength for the body area. A 2024 review of 291 trials found no extra skin thinning with short-term use.

items.name: Fingertip unit (FTU)
items.note: A line of cream from the tip of an adult's finger to the first crease, about 0.5 g. It covers two adult palms. Apply once or twice a day to red patches only.

items.name: Twice-weekly maintenance
items.note: After a flare settles, apply the cream twice a week to the usual spots. This prevents new flares.

items.name: Tacrolimus / pimecrolimus
items.note: Steroid-free creams that are good for the face, eyelids and folds. Burning settles after a few days. Large studies show no meaningful cancer risk.

items.name: Newer non-steroid creams
items.note: Ruxolitinib, roflumilast and tapinarof creams are approved overseas, but are not yet confirmed in South Africa. See Wonder Cures.

items.name: Topical steroid withdrawal (TSW)
items.note: Recognised but poorly understood. It is mostly linked to long-term misuse of strong steroids on the face or genitals. Follow your doctor's plan rather than stopping suddenly.

items.name: Habit reversal
items.note: When the urge to scratch hits, clench your fists or press on the spot for 30 seconds instead. Small trials show it helps.

items.name: Keep nails short
items.note: This reduces skin damage from scratching, especially at night. Cotton mittens help babies.

items.name: Be gentle
items.note: Use lukewarm short baths, pat dry and avoid scrubbing.

items.name: Soft, loose cotton clothing
items.note: Silk is not better than cotton (CLOTHES trial). Loose, breathable and soft is what matters.

items.name: "Just stop scratching"
items.note: This rarely works on its own. Control the itch with treatment and use habit reversal instead.

items.name: Written eczema action plan
items.note: Ask your doctor for one. The Allergy Foundation of South Africa has a template.

items.name: Phototherapy (narrowband UVB)
items.note: Medical light treatment at a dermatologist for widespread eczema. This is not the same as sunbathing or sunbeds.

items.name: Ciclosporin
items.note: Fast-acting tablet for severe eczema. Short-term only, with kidney and blood pressure checks. Avoid grapefruit.

items.name: Methotrexate
items.note: An effective option needing regular blood tests. Keep alcohol to a minimum. It is not registered for eczema in South Africa (used off-label).

items.name: Oral steroids (prednisone, cortisone)
items.note: Guidelines advise against them, strongly so for children. They cause rebound flares and side effects. Specialist short rescue only.

items.name: Non-drowsy antihistamines
items.note: They don't reliably help eczema itch (Cochrane review). They are useful for hay fever or hives.

items.name: Drowsy antihistamine at night
items.note: Only a short 7–14 day trial during a flare that ruins sleep, on a doctor's advice. Promethazine (Phenergan) must not be used under 2 years.

items.name: Coal tar
items.note: An old treatment with weak evidence. It stains, smells and makes skin sun-sensitive. Use it only on specialist advice.

items.name: Dust-mite covers
items.note: No reliable benefit for most people (Cochrane). They might help only people with a proven dust-mite allergy.

items.name: Food elimination diets
items.note: Only remove a food if an allergy is confirmed by a doctor. Avoid internet and high-street allergy tests.

items.name: Tea tree oil in the bath
items.note: A common skin allergen that can make eczema worse.

sections.title: See a doctor the same day if…
sections.intro:
• Eczema suddenly gets worse, weeps, crusts or has yellow spots (possible infection).
• There are painful, punched-out blisters or sores, especially with fever. This could be eczema herpeticum, a medical emergency.
• A baby's eczema is severe or not settling.

categories.title: Remedies
categories.subtitle: Home and natural remedies: what's worth trying
categories.intro: Natural doesn't always mean gentle. Some popular remedies are common skin allergens. Use these alongside your prescribed treatment, never instead of it. Patch-test anything new on a small area for a few days.

items.name: Vaseline (petroleum jelly)
items.note: Cheap, effective and fragrance-free. Recommended by South African guidance.

items.name: Virgin coconut oil
items.note: Beat mineral oil in a trial of 117 children with mild–moderate eczema, and may reduce staph bacteria. Don't use it on infected skin.

items.name: Sunflower seed oil
items.note: Helped preserve the skin barrier in a study. A good natural oil option.

items.name: Colloidal oatmeal
items.note: Gives temporary itch relief. Choose fragrance-free products, and stop if it stings.

items.name: Wet wraps after a bath
items.note: Very helpful for bad flares, short-term, with a doctor or nurse's guidance. Never use them on infected skin.

items.name: Shop-bought ointments and creams
items.note: Plain fragrance-free emollients are fine. Avoid unlabelled or imported "eczema creams": some secretly contain steroids.

sections.title: Unproven: try with care
sections.intro: No good eczema trials. Harmless for many people, but stop if your skin reacts.

items.name: Aloe vera gel
items.note: No trials of aloe alone. Many gels contain alcohol or fragrance. Allergy has been reported.

items.name: Shea butter
items.note: A reasonable plain moisturiser if you tolerate it. No eczema trials.

items.name: Cassia alata
items.note: Antibacterial in the lab only. No human eczema studies.

items.name: Castor oil
items.note: No eczema trials, and contact allergy has been reported.

items.name: Black seed oil (Nigella sativa)
items.note: One small trial, but severe allergic skin reactions have been reported. Never apply it undiluted. Oral use is unproven.

items.name: Speensalf (udder cream)
items.note: A veterinary teat ointment for dairy cows. Its ingredients vary and it isn't made for eczema. Use a fragrance-free emollient instead.

items.name: Calendula and chamomile
items.note: Daisy-family plants. Allergy to them is more common in people with eczema.

items.name: Honey / manuka
items.note: Only a tiny uncontrolled study. Never give honey to babies under 1.

items.name: Hemp / CBD creams
items.note: One small trial. Products vary and are unregulated.

items.name: Rooibos on the skin
items.note: Promising in mouse studies only.

items.name: Tea tree oil
items.note: A well-known skin allergen, and worse in old bottles. It can make eczema flare.

items.name: Turmeric on the skin
items.note: A proven contact allergen that also stains. Eating it in food is fine.

items.name: Apple cider vinegar
items.note: In a 2019 study it didn't help the skin barrier and irritated most people's skin.

items.name: Olive oil
items.note: Damaged the skin barrier in a study. Avoid it for baby massage too.

items.name: Milk of magnesia
items.note: No evidence. It is alkaline, and eczema skin prefers slightly acidic products.

items.name: Worcestershire sauce
items.note: No evidence. The vinegar and spices sting and irritate broken skin.

items.name: Witch hazel
items.note: No eczema evidence, and many products contain drying alcohol.

categories.title: Supplements
categories.subtitle: Vitamins, pills and products: what the evidence says
categories.intro: Most supplements have not been shown to help eczema. Vitamin D (if low or in winter) and short-term melatonin for sleep are the only ones with modest support. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take.

items.name: Vitamin D
items.note: Gave a modest improvement in trials, mainly in people with low levels or in winter. Ask for a blood test, and don't megadose.

items.name: Melatonin
items.note: Helped children with eczema fall asleep about 21 minutes faster. Short-term only, with a doctor's dose.

items.name: Vitamin B12 cream (on the skin)
items.note: Small placebo-controlled trials showed improvement. Oral B12 liquid has no evidence unless you are deficient.

sections.title: No proven benefit
sections.intro: Probably harmless at normal doses, but probably not worth the money for eczema.

items.name: Probiotics
items.note: Probably make little or no difference to eczema (Cochrane review of 39 trials).

items.name: Omega-3 / fish oil
items.note: No clinically meaningful benefit in reviews. Eating oily fish as food is still healthy.

items.name: Vitamin C
items.note: No proven benefit, but no evidence it harms eczema either. High-strength skin serums may sting.

items.name: Vitamin E
items.note: No benefit found in reviews.

items.name: Zinc & copper
items.note: May help only if you are truly deficient. There are no copper studies.

items.name: Calcium & magnesium
items.note: No eczema trials found.

items.name: Milk thistle
items.note: No evidence it relieves itch.

items.name: L-lysine, chlorophyll, quercetin, collagen
items.note: No eczema trials found.

items.name: Evening primrose & borage oil
items.note: No better than placebo across 27 trials (Cochrane).

items.name: "Liver detox" supplements
items.note: No link between liver detox and eczema. Some herbal mixtures have caused liver damage.

items.name: Non-drowsy antihistamines for eczema itch
items.note: No consistent benefit for eczema. Only useful for hay fever or hives.

items.name: Phenergan (promethazine) every night
items.note: Not for routine use. Never give it under 2 years (it can stop breathing), and tablets are not for under 5. Short flare use only, on prescription.

items.name: Prednisone / cortisone tablets
items.note: Not a supplement. These are prescription steroids that guidelines advise against for eczema because they cause rebound flares.

items.name: Retinol skin products
items.note: Dries and irritates eczema skin. Not for use in pregnancy.

items.name: Fragrance & perfumes
items.note: Among the most common skin allergens. Choose unperfumed products.

categories.title: Causes & Triggers
categories.subtitle: Why eczema happens and what sets off flares
categories.intro: Eczema's root causes are genes, a weak skin barrier and an over-reactive immune system. Triggers then set off flares, and they differ from person to person. Keeping a simple diary of flares helps you spot your own pattern.

items.name: Genes and family history
items.note: Eczema runs in families with eczema, asthma or hay fever.

items.name: Skin barrier (filaggrin)
items.note: Some people's skin lacks strong building blocks, so water escapes and irritants get in.

items.name: Immune system
items.note: An over-reactive allergy-type response causes redness and itch.

sections.title: Irritants
sections.intro: These damage everyone's skin, and eczema skin most of all.

items.name: Soaps, detergents, bubble baths
items.note: Use a soap-free wash and avoid anything that foams.

items.name: Perfumes and fragrance
items.note: Both an irritant and a common allergen. Choose fragrance-free creams, washes and washing powder.

items.name: Scratchy or rough fabrics
items.note: Coarse wool and tight, hot clothing itch. Soft, loose cotton is best.

items.name: Tobacco smoke
items.note: Second-hand smoke is a known trigger. Keep homes and cars smoke-free.

items.name: Paraffin, coal and wood smoke, traffic fumes
items.note: Linked to more eczema in South African studies. Ventilate well when using indoor fuels.

items.name: Reactions to creams
items.note: If controlled eczema suddenly worsens after a new product, ask about patch testing for contact allergy.

items.name: Heat and sweat
items.note: Keep cool and don't overdress babies. Rinse sweat off and moisturise, but don't avoid exercise.

items.name: Dry air and cold
items.note: Highveld winters dry the skin, so moisturise more often in dry or cold weather.

items.name: House dust mites
items.note: Only matters if you're allergic. Mite-proofing helps little for most people, so don't buy costly products just in case.

items.name: Pollen
items.note: Relevant if you're allergic, often with seasonal or eye-area flares. Ask about testing.

items.name: Pet fur and dander
items.note: Avoid pets only if an allergy is proven. Early-life contact with dogs is linked to less eczema.

items.name: Damp and mould
items.note: May worsen allergies. Fix damp for general health, although evidence for eczema itself is limited.

items.name: Hard water
items.note: Water softeners didn't help eczema in a large trial. South African metro water is mostly soft.

items.name: Stress, including family or relationship stress
items.note: Stress worsens itch, and eczema adds stress. It is a two-way link, so support and coping skills help.

items.name: Hormones
items.note: Some women flare in the week before a period or during pregnancy. Plan extra skin care then.

items.name: Staph infection
items.note: Weeping, crusting or yellow spots mean possible infection. See a doctor.

items.name: Eczema herpeticum (emergency)
items.note: Painful clustered blisters or punched-out sores, often with fever. Get medical help the same day.

items.name: Yeast (Malassezia)
items.note: Head and neck eczema in some teens and adults may respond to antifungal treatment.

items.name: Baby with gut symptoms
items.note: Eczema plus vomiting, colic, diarrhoea or poor growth? Ask your doctor about food allergy.

items.name: "Gut health" / leaky gut
items.note: Gut bacteria may differ in eczema, but probiotics don't reliably help and "leaky gut" isn't a recognised diagnosis.

items.name: Candida
items.note: No good evidence that gut thrush causes eczema or that anti-candida diets help.

items.name: Liver, spleen, "detox"
items.note: Eczema is not caused by liver or spleen problems. Some herbal cleanses can harm the liver or contain hidden steroids.

items.name: Gluten
items.note: Not a common eczema trigger. Guidelines advise against going gluten-free unless coeliac disease or a wheat allergy is diagnosed.

items.name: Myth: a healthy diet can cure eczema
items.note: Fact: healthy eating is great for general health, but no diet cures eczema, and cutting foods can cause new allergies.

items.name: Myth: eczema heals naturally
items.note: Fact: many children improve with age, but not all, and flares often return. Untreated eczema harms sleep and skin. Herbal "natural cures" are unproven.

items.name: Myth: eczema is contagious
items.note: Fact: you cannot catch eczema. Infected eczema can spread germs, so keep skin treated and hands clean.

items.name: Myth: only children get eczema
items.note: Fact: there is a second peak in older adults, and it can start at any age.

items.name: Myth: steroid creams always thin the skin
items.note: Fact: thinning is rare when they are used as directed, even with twice-weekly preventive use.

items.name: Myth: children with eczema shouldn't be vaccinated
items.note: Fact: vaccinate on schedule. Only some strong eczema tablets affect live vaccines, so ask your doctor.

categories.title: Drinks & Beverages
categories.subtitle: What to drink, and what to keep for treats
categories.intro: No drink has been proven to cure or calm eczema, and very few drinks need to be avoided. Hydrate your skin from the outside with moisturiser. Choose drinks for good sleep and general health.

items.name: Water
items.note: The best everyday drink. It won't moisturise eczema skin on its own; moisturiser does that.

items.name: Rooibos
items.note: Caffeine-free and family-friendly. Lab studies look interesting, but there is no human proof that it calms eczema.

items.name: Green tea
items.note: Fine to drink. The skin benefits seen in studies came mostly from creams, not from cups of tea. Contains caffeine.

items.name: Oolong tea
items.note: One small, uncontrolled 2001 study suggested a benefit. It is not proven, but fine to drink if you enjoy it.

items.name: Black tea
items.note: No evidence it worsens eczema. Contains caffeine, so it is not for babies and young children.

items.name: Cow's milk
items.note: Only cut it out if a doctor confirms a milk allergy. Removing it unnecessarily can harm nutrition and may even raise allergy risk.

items.name: Plant milks (soya, oat, almond)
items.note: Choose unsweetened, calcium-fortified versions from age 1. No rice drinks for under-5s.

items.name: Coconut milk drink
items.note: No eczema evidence either way. It is not a complete milk replacement for children, so ask a dietitian.

items.name: Kefir and probiotic drinks
items.note: Fine as food, but probiotics have not been shown to treat eczema (Cochrane review).

items.name: Bone broth
items.note: No evidence it helps eczema. Fine as food.

items.name: Coffee
items.note: No proven link to eczema. Avoid it later in the day, because poor sleep makes itch worse. Not for children.

items.name: Matcha
items.note: Fine for adults, but high in caffeine. Avoid it late in the day and don't give it to children.

items.name: Fruit juice (apple, grape, citrus)
items.note: No eczema effect, but sugary. Dilute 1 part juice to 10 parts water for young children and give with meals. Citrus can redden skin around a toddler's mouth.

items.name: Vegetable juice (beet, celery)
items.note: No proven benefit. Celery is an allergen for some people. Handling a lot of celery in the sun can cause a skin reaction.

items.name: Smoothies
items.note: Fine. For children, dilute and serve with meals. Leave out any food with a confirmed allergy.

items.name: Kombucha
items.note: No human evidence of benefit. It is acidic, often sugary and can contain a little alcohol. Adults only.

items.name: Soda and fizzy drinks
items.note: There is no direct eczema link, but they are bad for teeth and general health. Not for young children.

items.name: Energy drinks (under 18)
items.note: Linked to short, poor-quality sleep and other harms in young people. Adults should keep them occasional.

items.name: Grapefruit juice on certain medicines
items.note: Avoid it if you take ciclosporin or upadacitinib (Rinvoq), because it raises medicine levels in the blood. Check every medicine leaflet.

sections.title: Alcohol
sections.intro: There's no strong proof that alcohol causes eczema flares. It can make skin flush and itch, and it disturbs sleep, which makes itch worse. Red wine, beer and darker spirits contain more histamine, sulphites or congeners, and people notice them most. If you drink, keep it light and drink water in between.

items.name: Gin, vodka, silver (blanco) tequila
items.note: Clear spirits are lowest in congeners. Use plain mixers such as soda water, and stop a few hours before bed.

items.name: Red wine
items.note: The alcohol most often reported to trigger itch and flushing, because of its histamine and sulphites.

items.name: White and sparkling wine
items.note: Lower in histamine than red, but still contains sulphites.

items.name: Beer and cider
items.note: Fermented and containing biogenic amines. Some people notice flushing or itch.

items.name: Brandy, whisky, dark rum
items.note: Darker spirits contain more congeners and are linked to worse hangovers. Keep them occasional.

items.name: Sake and rice wines
items.note: Fermented like wine and beer, not a clear spirit. Treat sake like wine.

items.name: Cocktails, alcopops, liqueurs
items.note: Lots of sugar and mixed ingredients, which makes triggers hard to track. No grapefruit cocktails on ciclosporin or Rinvoq.

items.name: Under 18, pregnant or breastfeeding
items.note: Avoid alcohol completely. Drinking in pregnancy is linked to eczema in the child.

items.name: On methotrexate or ciclosporin
items.note: Keep alcohol to a minimum, because methotrexate and alcohol both strain the liver. Ask your doctor or pharmacist.

categories.title: Food
categories.subtitle: Eating well with eczema: no special diet needed
categories.intro: There is no special eczema diet. Eat a varied, balanced diet, and only remove a food if a doctor or allergist confirms an allergy. If you must cut out a major food such as milk, use a dietitian. Treat the skin first.

items.name: Oily fish (pilchards, snoek, sardines, mackerel)
items.note: Healthy fats. Fish in a baby's first year is linked to less eczema. (Fish-oil capsules don't treat eczema.)

items.name: Amasi, maas and plain yoghurt
items.note: Fermented milk was linked to less eczema in South African toddlers. Fine unless you are allergic to milk.

items.name: Vegetables and fruit
items.note: Butternut, sweet potato, pumpkin, spinach and morogo are all great. No evidence they worsen eczema.

items.name: Mediterranean-style eating
items.note: Legumes, whole grains, olive or canola oil and nuts. Linked to milder eczema in one study. Good for overall health.

items.name: Lean meat, chicken, beans and lentils
items.note: Good sources of protein and iron.

sections.title: Babies: introduce allergens early
sections.intro: Giving babies smooth peanut and well-cooked egg early, from about 4–6 months, lowers the chance of allergy. In the LEAP trial, peanut allergy fell from 13.7% to 1.9%. If your baby has severe eczema, speak to your doctor first.

items.name: Well-cooked egg (from about 4–6 months)
items.note: Early, regular feeding lowers egg allergy risk.

items.name: Smooth peanut butter (from about 4–6 months)
items.note: Thin it with water or breast milk. Never give whole nuts under 5, because they are a choking risk.

items.name: Mother avoiding foods while pregnant or breastfeeding
items.note: Not recommended unless the baby has a proven allergy and a doctor advises it.

items.name: Mielie pap, samp, rice
items.note: No evidence maize worsens eczema. Add vegetables and protein.

items.name: Bread, wheat and gluten
items.note: No benefit from going gluten-free unless coeliac disease or a wheat allergy is diagnosed.

items.name: Oats (eating)
items.note: Eating oats is fine. Oat creams may sensitise some babies with broken skin.

items.name: Milk, cheese and butter
items.note: Fine unless a cow's milk allergy is diagnosed. Children need the calcium.

items.name: Eggs
items.note: Eat them normally unless an egg allergy is proven. Eggs are not dairy.

items.name: Nuts and peanuts
items.note: Not an eczema cause in people who aren't allergic.

items.name: Soya
items.note: Fine unless you are allergic. Soya formula only on medical advice, and not before 6 months.

items.name: Sugar and sweets
items.note: Not an eczema cause (sugar has no histamine), but limit for teeth and weight.

items.name: Fast food and takeaways
items.note: Frequent fast food (3+ times a week) is linked to more severe eczema in surveys.

items.name: Boerewors, polony, viennas
items.note: Salty and fatty, and fried meats were linked to allergy in a South African study. Enjoy occasionally.

items.name: Biltong and droëwors
items.note: No eczema evidence either way. Very salty, so keep it moderate.

items.name: Citrus, tomato, strawberries (messy eaters)
items.note: The juice can redden skin around the mouth. This is usually irritation, not allergy. Apply barrier ointment before meals.

sections.title: Avoid only if a doctor confirms an allergy
sections.intro: Food allergy usually shows within 2 hours: hives, swelling, vomiting or wheeze. A positive skin or blood test alone does not prove allergy. Internet and IgG "intolerance" tests have no value.

items.name: Cow's milk (confirmed allergy)
items.note: The most common infant allergen. Use special formula only on medical advice, and retest after 6–12 months.

items.name: Egg (confirmed allergy)
items.note: Common in South African children with eczema. Many outgrow it, so recheck after 1–2 years.

items.name: Peanut and tree nuts (confirmed allergy)
items.note: Risk of severe reactions. Carry an emergency plan if allergic.

items.name: Wheat, soya, fish, shellfish (confirmed allergy)
items.note: Recognised allergens. Avoid them only after proper testing.

items.name: Elimination diets "just in case"
items.note: Little benefit, with a real risk of poor growth and new, sometimes severe allergies.

items.name: Low-histamine, low-nickel, anti-candida, detox diets
items.note: Not validated for eczema. Risk of poor nutrition.

items.name: IgG food "intolerance" tests
items.note: No evidence of value. They lead to unnecessary food bans.

categories.title: Water & Bathing
categories.subtitle: Bathing, showering, swimming and wet wraps
categories.intro: How you bathe matters more than how often. A 2025 trial of 438 people found daily and weekly bathing worked equally well. Use lukewarm water, keep it short, skip the soap, and moisturise straight after.

sections.title: Everyday bath or shower: soak and seal
sections.intro:
1. Lukewarm water (test with your wrist), 5–10 minutes.
2. Wash with an emollient or soap-free wash. Don't scrub.
3. Pat dry with a soft towel, leaving skin slightly damp.
4. Within about 3 minutes, put prescribed cream on the eczema patches and moisturiser everywhere else.
5. Dress in loose cotton.

items.name: Bath or shower, as often as suits you
items.note: Daily or a few times a week both work. What matters is moisturising straight afterwards.

items.name: Lukewarm water, 5–10 minutes
items.note: Hot water and long soaks make itch worse.

items.name: Moisturise within 3 minutes
items.note: Seal in the water while the skin is still damp.

items.name: Emollient instead of soap
items.note: Ordinary soap, bubble bath and shower gel strip the skin. Don't use aqueous cream: it irritates.

items.name: Pat dry, don't rub
items.note: Use a clean, soft towel. Don't share towels during an infected flare.

items.name: Hot showers and long baths
items.note: Heat triggers itch and dries the skin.

items.name: Bubble bath, scented gels, soap
items.note: Fragrance and detergents irritate eczema skin.

items.name: Dilute bleach bath (moderate–severe eczema)
items.note: Probably reduces severity (10 trials). Only with your doctor's OK, usually 2–3 times a week. See the recipe below.

items.name: Colloidal oatmeal
items.note: May soothe some people. Stop if it stings, because some people are sensitive to oats.

items.name: Dead Sea salt
items.note: One small study showed better skin hydration. Can sting broken skin. Optional, not a treatment.

items.name: Epsom salt or baking soda
items.note: No real eczema evidence. May sting. Optional.

items.name: Rooibos in the bath
items.note: Promising in mouse studies only. Harmless to try, but stop if it irritates.

items.name: Emollient bath oils
items.note: No benefit on top of normal moisturising (BATHE trial), and they make the bath slippery. Spend the money on leave-on moisturiser instead.

items.name: Vinegar soaks
items.note: No benefit, and most people got irritated skin in testing.

items.name: Tea tree oil in the bath
items.note: A common skin allergen, and old bottles are worse. Risky on broken eczema skin.

sections.title: Bleach bath: South African recipe
sections.intro:
Only if your doctor recommends it. Aim for about 0.005% bleach.

Jik is about 3.5% (check your bottle and use the plain, unscented one). That means 1.4 mL of bleach per litre of water:
• Baby bath (~15 L): about 21 mL (1 tablespoon + 1 teaspoon)
• Half bath (~80 L): about 115 mL (just under ½ cup)
• Full bath (~150 L): about 215 mL

US recipes use stronger 6% bleach, so don't copy their cup measures. Mix the bleach into lukewarm water before getting in. Soak 5–10 minutes and keep the water away from the eyes. Pat dry and moisturise straight away. Never mix bleach with other cleaners.

items.name: Water softener
items.note: Didn't help eczema even in very hard water (SWET trial). Johannesburg and Cape Town water is soft anyway.

items.name: Shower filter
items.note: No studies show it helps eczema. Not worth buying for eczema.

items.name: Borehole water
items.note: It can be much harder than municipal water. A lab hardness test is cheap if you're curious, but softeners still haven't been shown to help.

items.name: Swimming pool (chlorine)
items.note: Most people with eczema can swim. Moisturise before, then shower and moisturise straight after.

items.name: Sea swimming
items.note: Fine if it's comfortable, but it may sting cracked skin. Rinse in fresh water and moisturise afterwards.

items.name: Sunscreen outdoors
items.note: Choose a fragrance-free mineral (zinc or titanium) sunscreen if others sting.

sections.title: Wet wraps (for flares)
sections.intro:
Get a doctor or nurse to show you first. Never wrap infected eczema: weeping, crusting or yellow spots.
1. Bath, pat dry, and apply prescribed cream and moisturiser.
2. Dampen a cotton layer in warm water and wring it out until it is damp, not dripping.
3. Put it on, with a dry layer and loose pyjamas over the top.
4. Leave it on for 2 hours or overnight, then moisturise again.
5. Use for about 7–14 days, then review with your doctor.

items.name: Wet wrap therapy
items.note: Calms bad flares and helps sleep. Short-term only, because it increases steroid absorption.

items.name: Stay hydrated
items.note: Good for overall health, but drinking extra water won't fix dry eczema skin. Moisturiser will.

categories.title: Clothing & Laundry
categories.subtitle: Fabrics, fit and washing that keep skin calm
categories.intro: Aim for loose, soft and breathable clothing. No fabric treats eczema: even special silk clothing added no benefit in a 300-child trial. But the wrong fabrics, finishes and detergents can make itch worse.

items.name: 100% cotton
items.note: Soft, cool and absorbs sweat. Check labels, because "cotton-rich" can be mostly polyester.

items.name: Superfine merino (17.5 micron or finer)
items.note: Did better than cotton in two small trials (both wool-industry funded). Try one base layer first.

items.name: Bamboo viscose and TENCEL (lyocell)
items.note: Soft, smooth and absorbent. Eczema-friendly, though there are no trials.

items.name: Silk, including "eczema" silk garments
items.note: Comfortable if you like it, but not a treatment (CLOTHES trial). Spend money on moisturiser first.

items.name: Wicking sportswear
items.note: Well-fitting technical synthetics are OK for sport. Cotton, bamboo or merino may still feel gentler.

items.name: Polyester and synthetics (everyday)
items.note: Trap heat and sweat for many people, which sets off itch.

items.name: Lace, sequins, denim, fake fur
items.note: Common irritants. They're fine over a soft layer, but not directly on eczema.

items.name: Coarse wool next to the skin (jerseys, blankets)
items.note: Thick fibres prick and itch. This is irritation, not allergy, so wear wool over a cotton layer.

items.name: Loose fit
items.note: Tight clothes rub and trap heat. Size up for uniforms and workwear.

items.name: Cut out labels
items.note: Snip close to the seam, or buy tagless.

items.name: Rough seams
items.note: Wear the garment inside-out or tape over seams that irritate.

items.name: "Non-iron" and "wrinkle-free" finishes
items.note: Often treated with formaldehyde resins, a known clothing allergen.

items.name: Dark or bleeding dyes
items.note: Disperse dyes are leading textile allergens. A rash in the body folds is worth a patch test.

items.name: Nickel jeans studs and belt buckles
items.note: A rash under the navel stud suggests nickel allergy. Cover the stud with fabric tape and ask for a patch test.

items.name: Wash new clothes before wearing
items.note: This removes excess dye and finishing chemicals. Include school uniforms and bedding.

items.name: Fragrance-free detergent
items.note: Choose "fragrance-free" rather than "unscented", which can contain masking perfume.

items.name: Use less detergent and add an extra rinse
items.note: Overdosing leaves residue on fabric. Try this before switching brands.

items.name: Bio or non-bio
items.note: Either is fine. Enzymes caused no irritation or sensitisation in large studies.

items.name: Fabric softener
items.note: Some people tolerate it and some don't. Use fragrance-free only, and test it separately.

items.name: Change one product at a time
items.note: Give each change a month. Detergent often gets blamed for flares it didn't cause.

items.name: Monthly hot empty wash
items.note: A 90 °C empty cycle clears emollient build-up and bacteria in the machine.

items.name: Cotton gloves or mittens at night
items.note: They reduce damage from scratching during sleep. All-in-one sleepsuits with mitts help children.

items.name: Breathable sleepwear and cotton sheets
items.note: Use light layers you can peel off, and keep the room cool (16–18 °C).

items.name: Spiky roller balls
items.note: No evidence they help, and they may damage broken skin. Try pressing, pinching or a cold pack instead.

items.name: Fire safety
items.note: Emollient-soaked clothes and bedding burn easily. No smoking in bed and no candles near the bed. Wash bedding often.

items.name: Sun-protective clothing and a hat
items.note: UPF clothing means less sunscreen is needed on sensitive skin.

items.name: Sport kit
items.note: Wear breathable layers you can remove, wash kit after every session and shower soon after.

items.name: School uniforms
items.note: Buy loose, remove tags, wash before wearing and add a cotton layer underneath.

categories.title: Health
categories.subtitle: Skin routine, sleep, exercise, infections and more
categories.intro: Eczema affects more than skin: sleep, mood, eyes and allergies too. These everyday habits and warning signs help keep the whole person well.

sections.title: See a doctor today if…
sections.intro:
• Eczema suddenly becomes painful with clustered blisters or small punched-out sores, often with fever. This could be eczema herpeticum, an emergency. Near the eyes, an eye doctor is needed too.
• There is weeping, pus, yellow crusts, rapid worsening or fever: possible bacterial infection.
Emergency numbers: 10177 (ambulance) · 112 (from a cellphone).

items.name: Moisturise every day, even when clear
items.note: At least twice a day, and 3–4 times is ideal. Adults with widespread eczema may use about 500 g a week.

items.name: Soak and seal
items.note: A short lukewarm wash, pat dry, medicine on red patches, then moisturiser everywhere else within 3 minutes.

items.name: Smooth on, don't rub
items.note: Apply in the direction of hair growth. Rubbing heats the skin.

items.name: Use a spoon or pump
items.note: Keep fingers out of tubs, and replace opened tubs after an infection.

items.name: Short, smooth nails
items.note: Check them weekly. Less damage when scratching happens anyway.

items.name: Cool emollient from the fridge
items.note: Soothing on itchy skin. Never warm emollients in the microwave.

items.name: Cool bedroom (16–18 °C)
items.note: Heat drives night itch. Use a fan in summer and light layers you can adjust.

items.name: Thick moisturiser before bed
items.note: Apply it well before lights-out so you don't overheat.

items.name: Regular bedtime, screens off an hour before
items.note: Good sleep habits help eczema sleepers too. Avoid late caffeine and alcohol.

items.name: Melatonin
items.note: Helped children fall asleep faster, with only a small effect on the skin. Ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

items.name: Regularly losing sleep
items.note: A sign the eczema is not controlled. Go back to the doctor, because treatment can be stepped up.

items.name: Regular exercise
items.note: It reduces stress and improves sleep and mood. Don't avoid sport because of eczema.

items.name: Plan for sweat
items.note: Wear layers, take breaks and drink cool water. Shower and moisturise soon after.

items.name: Sit out during infection or raw skin
items.note: This protects broken skin.

items.name: Sun: protect, don't burn
items.note: Some people improve in sunlight and others flare. Never aim to tan or burn. Stay in the shade from 11:00 to 15:00.

items.name: Mineral sunscreen SPF30+
items.note: Fragrance-free zinc oxide or titanium dioxide is often gentler. Patch-test a new one for 3–5 days.

items.name: Medical light therapy
items.note: Narrowband UVB at a dermatologist is a real treatment. It is not the same as sunbathing.

items.name: Highveld winter
items.note: Very dry air and heaters. Use a thicker moisturiser more often, keep showers lukewarm and don't sit close to heaters.

items.name: Coastal humidity and heat waves
items.note: Sweat and heat drive itch. Use lighter creams by day, loose cotton and a cool shower.

items.name: Smog and veld-fire days
items.note: Pollution is linked to flares. Stay indoors where practical and rinse skin afterwards.

items.name: Load-shedding
items.note: Keep a battery fan, a cold pack in a cooler box and a pump bottle of moisturiser by the bed.

items.name: Routine vaccines
items.note: Eczema is not a reason to skip or delay vaccines. Steroid creams aren't either.

items.name: Live vaccines on Dupixent or JAK tablets
items.note: Avoid live vaccines (e.g. MMR, yellow fever) during treatment. Get up to date before starting, and plan travel vaccines with the specialist.

items.name: Old smallpox vaccine (ACAM2000)
items.note: Not for people with eczema or their household contacts. The newer mpox vaccine (JYNNEOS) is fine.

items.name: Asthma, hay fever, itchy eyes
items.note: Part of the same "atopic" family. They deserve their own treatment.

items.name: Food allergy (mainly children)
items.note: Linked to early, severe eczema. Don't cut foods without a doctor (see Food).

items.name: Low mood and anxiety
items.note: Common and treatable, and not a weakness. See Motivation for support numbers.

items.name: Eyes: don't rub
items.note: Eczema and eye rubbing each roughly triple the risk of keratoconus. See an optometrist if vision blurs.

items.name: Sore or red eyes on Dupixent
items.note: A common, usually mild side effect. Report it early, because eye drops usually help.

items.name: Bone, heart and weight
items.note: Small links in adults. Have the usual health checks with your GP.

items.name: Written eczema action plan
items.note: Green is daily care, amber is flare steps, red is call the doctor. Ask your doctor to fill one in.

items.name: Weekly POEM score
items.note: Seven questions about the last week, scored 0–28: 0–2 clear, 3–7 mild, 8–16 moderate, 17–24 severe, 25–28 very severe.

items.name: Weekly photos
items.note: Same areas, same light. Note itch and sleep too, because redness is harder to see on darker skin.

items.name: Who to see
items.note: Pharmacist for mild patches. GP if treatment isn't working or sleep is disturbed. Dermatologist for frequent flares or suspected contact allergy.

categories.title: Motivation & Affirmations
categories.subtitle: For the person with eczema, and the people who love him
categories.intro: Eczema is tiring in ways others don't always see: broken sleep, constant itch, stares and endless routines. Feeling low is common and treatable. And treatments today are better than ever.

sections.title: Need to talk? (South Africa)
sections.intro: If anyone talks about not wanting to live, call together. Don't wait.

items.name: SADAG Suicide Crisis Helpline
items.note: Free, 24 hours.

items.name: Cipla Mental Health Helpline
items.note: 24 hours. You can also SMS 31393 or WhatsApp 076 882 2775 (8am–5pm).

items.name: Adcock Ingram Depression & Anxiety Helpline
items.note: 8am–8pm.

items.name: Dr Reddy's Mental Health Helpline
items.note: 8am–8pm.

items.name: Emergency (life in danger)
items.note: Ambulance 10177 · from a cellphone 112.

sections.title: Daily affirmations
sections.intro: Pick one for today. Say it, write it, or stick it on the mirror.

items.name: My skin is one part of me, not the whole of me.
I can have a hard skin day and still have a good day.
A flare is weather, not a verdict.
Itchy moments pass. I have ways to get through them.
I have lived with this for years, and that makes me strong, not broken.
Taking care of my skin is self-respect, not a chore I failed at.
Today I'll do what I can, and that is enough.
I am more than the itch.
Bad nights don't cancel good days.
I deserve comfort: soft clothes, cool air and kind words.
My worth isn't measured by how my skin looks.
I don't owe anyone an explanation for my skin.
I'm allowed to rest when my body is tired.
Asking for help is a skill, and I'm getting better at it.
I can be patient with my skin and with myself.
Every routine I keep is a small win worth noticing.
I'm learning what my body needs, one week at a time.
People who love me want to help, and I can let them.
I can feel frustrated and still be hopeful.
I choose gentleness over blame today.
There is no perfect routine, only the one I keep coming back to.
I can speak up to my doctor. My experience matters.
I'm proud of how I keep showing up.
I'm allowed to say no to advice that doesn't help me.
My family is on my team.
I can take this one hour at a time.
I make room for joy, even on itchy days.
Healing isn't a straight line, and that's okay.
More effective treatments exist than ever
items.note: Since 2023, guidelines have strongly recommended many new injections, tablets and creams. Ask a dermatologist what suits you.

items.name: Treating the skin helps the mind
items.note: Anxiety and depression scores improved when eczema treatment worked.

items.name: Mind tools are backed by trials
items.note: Online CBT and mindfulness with self-compassion helped adults, including people who had had eczema for about 27 years.

items.name: Small habits add up
items.note: Habit reversal plus usual treatment improved skin more than treatment alone.

items.name: "Not controlled" is a signal, not a sentence
items.note: If treatment isn't working, that's a reason to step up treatment, not a personal failure.

items.name: You're not alone
items.note: About 1 in 5 urban South African teens report eczema symptoms.

items.name: Talking therapy
items.note: Recommended by NICE when quality of life stays poor despite good skin treatment.

items.name: Mindfulness & self-compassion
items.note: An 8-week online programme improved quality of life and eczema severity in adults.

items.name: CBT (including online)
items.note: Reduced itch, stress, sleep problems and depression, with benefits lasting a year.

items.name: Habit reversal
items.note: When the urge hits, press, pinch or clench your fists and count to 10 instead of scratching.

items.name: Relaxation and breathing
items.note: Helps stress more than skin, but it's low-risk and worth trying.

items.name: Managing ongoing stress and conflict
items.note: Stress and itch feed each other. Support from family or a counsellor helps break the loop.

items.name: Say: "That looks itchy. Want the cold pack?"
items.note: Offers help without blame.

items.name: Avoid: "Stop scratching!"
items.note: Scratching is often automatic. Being told off adds stress, and stress adds itch.

items.name: Avoid: "Have you tried…?"
items.note: Unasked-for remedies are tiring. Ask instead: "Can I fetch anything from the pharmacy?"

items.name: Avoid: "It's just a rash" or "You'll grow out of it"
items.note: This minimises a lifelong condition. Try: "I know this is hard to live with."

items.name: Take one job off his plate
items.note: Reorder moisturiser, wash bedding, keep spare tubs in the car, or put cream on his back (ask first).

items.name: Learn the emergency signs
items.note: Know the signs of eczema herpeticum (see Health) so he isn't the only one watching.

items.name: Spot a bad week
items.note: Broken sleep, cancelled plans, long sleeves in the heat, skipped treatment or "what's the point". A gentle check-in helps.

items.name: Notice the wins
items.note: A calm night or a kept routine is worth naming.

glossary.detail: A highly recommended everyday choice, either for skin care or for general health. It does not mean a food or product cures eczema.
A habit or product that commonly makes eczema worse, such as hot showers, bubble bath or fragrance.
Used only where histamine plausibly matters, mainly wine and beer, which can trigger flushing and itch. "Histamine intolerance" diets are not proven to help eczema.
A root cause inside the body (genes, skin barrier, immune system), not something anyone did wrong.

glossary.meaning: The medical name for the most common type of eczema
glossary.detail: Long-lasting, itchy skin inflammation that comes and goes in flares. It isn't contagious.

glossary.meaning: A period when eczema gets worse
glossary.detail: Redder, itchier, sometimes weepy skin. Remission is when it settles.
Lotions, creams, gels and ointments that soften skin and repair the barrier. They are the foundation of all eczema care.

glossary.meaning: An emollient used to wash instead of soap
glossary.detail: Aqueous cream can be used to wash, but not as a leave-on moisturiser.

glossary.meaning: Moisturise within about 3 minutes of bathing
glossary.detail: Pat dry, put medicine on the patches, then moisturiser everywhere else, to lock water into the skin.
The first-choice treatment for flares. Strengths range from mild (e.g. hydrocortisone 1%) to very potent. Safe when used as directed.
A line of cream from the tip of an adult's index finger to the first crease (about 0.5 g). It covers two adult palms.
Steroid or tacrolimus cream applied twice a week to usual flare spots after the skin has settled, to prevent new flares.
Very common, and it leads to under-treated flares. Used correctly, the benefits outweigh the risks.
Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus: steroid-free creams that are good for the face, eyelids and folds.

glossary.meaning: An injected medicine that targets one part of the immune system
glossary.detail: E.g. dupilumab (Dupixent), tralokinumab, lebrikizumab, nemolizumab. For moderate–severe eczema.

glossary.meaning: A medicine that blocks inflammation signals inside cells
glossary.detail: Tablets (upadacitinib/Rinvoq, abrocitinib/Cibinqo, baricitinib) or creams (ruxolitinib). They work fast but need monitoring.

glossary.meaning: A damp cotton layer under a dry layer
glossary.detail: Used short-term for bad flares, with a doctor's guidance. Never on infected skin.
Can reduce severity in moderate–severe eczema, but only with a doctor's OK. See Water for the South African recipe.
Some people inherit weaker filaggrin, so water escapes and irritants get in.
Children with eczema are more likely to develop food allergy, asthma or hay fever, but many never do.
It thrives on eczema skin and can cause infection: weeping, yellow crusts, pus spots.

glossary.meaning: Eczema infected with the cold-sore virus
glossary.detail: An emergency: painful clustered blisters, punched-out sores, fever. Get seen the same day.

glossary.meaning: Two different ways things worsen eczema
glossary.detail: Irritants (soap, wool, sweat) bother everyone's skin. Allergens (pollen, nickel, some foods) only affect people who are allergic to them.

glossary.meaning: A positive test is not the same as an allergy
glossary.detail: Skin-prick or blood tests can be positive without real reactions. An oral food challenge is the gold standard.
Not recommended unless an allergy is confirmed. It can cause poor growth and new allergies.
Small amounts of allergens are taped to the back for a few days. It is useful when creams, fabrics or metals seem to cause reactions.
Seven questions about the past week, scored 0–28, that families can fill in at home to track eczema.
Used in clinics and trials to measure how much skin is affected and how badly.
Given at a dermatologist. It is not the same as sunbathing or sunbeds.

glossary.meaning: Swapping scratching for a harmless action
glossary.detail: Notice the urge, then press, pinch or clench your fists for 30 seconds instead of scratching.

glossary.meaning: Darker or lighter patches after eczema
glossary.detail: Common on darker skin. They fade slowly once the eczema is controlled.
